paras: The killing of James Hawkins was the fatal shooting of a Black striker by New Orleans Police Sergeant Reynolds on the morning of September 10, 1881, during a strike of the city's cotton laborers. Hawkins, a member of the Cotton Teamsters' Association, was shot during an attempted arrest of strikers who had interfered with teamsters hauling cotton. His death led the mayor to call for troops and produced a funeral that a press dispatch called the largest in the city since the war, attended by white and Black labor organizations.

In early September 1881 New Orleans cotton laborers were on strike, and the employers' association refused outside arbitration while seeking to compel a settlement on its own terms. Replacement workers had been brought in, among them Black laborers from Savannah.

According to the Associated Press wire, strikers interfered with wagons leaving Cooper's cotton press that morning, and when Sergeant Reynolds ordered them to disperse he was knocked down and beaten. He then drew his revolver and shot a Black striker through the head, killing him instantly, and the wire added that two white men were wounded. The Sun's fuller dispatch named the dead man as James Hawkins and said that during the attempted arrest Reynolds's clothing was torn off and Black women threw missiles at his head. In that version Reynolds fired two shots "as the prisoner was about to escape": one passed through Hawkins's thigh and struck a white man, Pat Connelly, in the leg, and the second hit Hawkins in the forehead.

Fire-alarm bells summoned the whole police force, several people were arrested for interfering with teamsters, and an abandoned float of cotton was set on fire. Mayor Shakespeare closed liquor places near the trouble and wrote to the Governor that the police had been "overpowered," and militia regiments were ordered to their armories but dismissed that afternoon.

Strikers met that night and resolved to give the dead man a "heroic burial" with white and Black workers taking part. On September 11 several thousand people gathered on Levee street at the house where Hawkins's body lay, and Black organizations with bands led a procession several blocks long to the grave. A wire report said every man in the line was armed in fear of an attack, which did not come, and called the union of Black and Irish laborers "unprecedented."

Some of the Black laborers recently brought from Savannah went to City Hall seeking means to return home after the killing. The Donaldsonville Chief reported that the strike ended in a compromise on the night of Tuesday, September 13, with the employers keeping the right to hire and discharge free of union dictation. No report of an inquest, charge or trial involving Sergeant Reynolds appears in the coverage.

Coverage came entirely from the white press, beginning on September 11 and running in weekly digests into late September. Headlines such as "Labor Riot in New Orleans" and "Rioting Strikers at New-Orleans" framed the event as strike disorder, and most papers printed the police version that the sergeant was attacked first. The Chicago Tribune blamed "evil-disposed persons" for the trouble, and the Louisiana Donaldsonville Chief wrote that Hawkins was killed "while resisting arrest" and faulted the militia for staying in their armories.

A Sept. 11 dispatch said the killing "seems to have had no other justification than the intimidation of the colored laborers," wording that can be read as naming Hawkins's alleged intimidation as the cause. The Daily Republican remarked that "the colored man of course was killed by the policeman" and that peace was restored "without the fun of killing a number more of colored men." Digest columns in Wisconsin and Dakota papers reprinted a version in which the sergeant was beaten with clubs and women fired at police from windows.

Accounts differ on why Reynolds fired: the AP said he had been knocked down and beaten, the Sun that Hawkins was about to escape, and the Chicago Tribune that he refused to submit to arrest. The wounded also vary, with the Sun naming one white man hit by the same bullet, the AP reporting two white men wounded, and a Sacramento summary saying two others were wounded.

reader.title: Killing of James Hawkins
bases: A named police sergeant shot James Hawkins dead during an attempted arrest of strikers interfering with cotton teamsters in a labor strike (A1, A6, A19).

The Sun's and Associated Press dispatches, a Chicago Tribune special and the Louisiana Donaldsonville Chief agree that Sergeant Reynolds shot and killed Hawkins, a Black striker, on Sept. 10, though they differ on the circumstances (A1, A2, A6, A19).

accounts.label: Associated Press wire, Sept. 10
accounts.gist: Strikers interfered with teamsters at Cooper's cotton press; ordered to disperse, Sergeant Reynolds was knocked down and beaten, drew his revolver and shot a Black striker through the head; two white men were wounded.

accounts.label: Fuller Sept. 10 dispatch (Sun)
accounts.gist: In the attempted arrest of Hawkins, Reynolds's clothing was torn off and Black women threw missiles; 'as the prisoner was about to escape' Reynolds fired twice, hitting Hawkins in the thigh and forehead and a white man, Pat Connelly, in the leg.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune special
accounts.gist: A policeman killed a Black striker who refused to submit to arrest; Capt. Minor was shot and stoned by Black women; militia sympathized with the strikers.

accounts.label: Weekly news digest
accounts.gist: Trouble began with epithets at cotton-float drivers; the sergeant was beaten with clubs and fired on the crowd, killing Hawkins; women shot at police from windows.

accounts.label: Sept. 11 dispatch
accounts.gist: The killing 'seems to have had no other justification' than intimidation of colored laborers, a phrase that can refer to Hawkins's alleged intimidation of laborers.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the AP version under headings such as 'Rioting Strikers at New-Orleans' and 'Becoming Violent—One of Them Killed', presenting the officer's beating as the cause.

The Chicago Tribune blamed 'evil-disposed persons' and called the dead man a striker who 'refused to submit to arrest'; the Donaldsonville Chief said he was killed 'while resisting arrest' and urged use of troops.
The Daily Republican's editorial remark that 'the colored man of course was killed' mocked the outcome and the militia rather than endorsing it.
The Sept. 11 and 12 dispatches dwelt on the large, interracial funeral and the union of Black and Irish laborers.
